message.reasoning:
I am playing as player p4 (grok-4.7) in Monopoly.

I have $639 and a yellow monopoly with one house on Ventnor and Marvin. Only Atlantic is buildable. Player 1 is bankrupt.

Player 2 has $312 and owns Boardwalk. They have no monopolies but own both utilities and two jail cards.

Player 3 has $3508 and is in jail after rolling a 7 without doubles.

Player 3 owns all four railroads and light blue properties with hotels. The brown monopoly is split between me and them.

Player 3 also owns Illinois, Pennsylvania Avenue, and Short Line. Their light blue hotels are extremely expensive. I cannot build on Atlantic because that would leave me with only $489, below the $600 cash threshold. I will not unmortgage the orange properties or Boardwalk either.

I will not trade my Mediterranean Avenue to player 3 or orange properties to player 2. From St James Place, the next roll lands on Tennessee through Illinois, so I will not hit light blue this turn. Player 3 is still in jail. I am now deciding whether to build, trade, mortgage, or end my turn.

Player 3's railroads are spaced far from St James Place. Illinois is only eight spaces away and unimproved rent is $20. B&O is nine spaces away. The next roll from here lands on Tennessee, New York, Free Parking, and Kentucky.

The worst possible rent from this position is $200 on B&O or $120 on Water Works. Both are easily covered by my $639 cash. Reaching the light blue properties would require at least three turns.

The immediate hotel threat is gone. I am now calculating exact rent values for the yellow monopoly to decide whether to build.

Building one house on Atlantic would cost $150 and leave me with $489. Player 2 is on Boardwalk, so he cannot land on the yellow properties this turn. Player 3 is in jail at space 10, which is 16 spaces from Atlantic.

Player 3 cannot reach the yellow properties in one roll, so building now is safe. The $150 cost leaves $489, which easily covers any upcoming railroad rent. The extra rent from one house on Atlantic would be only $66. I will likely have another decision point next turn.

Player 2 is too far away to threaten the yellow properties for several turns. Player 3 is still in jail and cannot reach them immediately.

I am weighing three paths to victory: build the yellow monopoly aggressively, unmortgage Boardwalk and complete the dark blue set, or bankrupt player 2 to claim his properties before facing player 3.

Player 2 would need about four turns to reach the yellow properties from Boardwalk. The orange monopoly is incomplete because St James Place and Tennessee Avenue are mortgaged, so no houses can be built there and the full orange rent does not apply.

The orange and dark blue monopolies are both incomplete. Orange only earns base rent on New York Avenue because St James Place and Tennessee Avenue remain mortgaged. Dark blue only earns base rent on Park Place since Boardwalk is mortgaged.

Yellow is the only buildable monopoly. I will build one house on Atlantic for $150, leaving $489. Then I can add a second house to each yellow property for $450, leaving $39. This completes the yellow set and maximizes rent against opponents.

Building one house on each yellow property would leave only $189, which is too little to cover a $200 railroad rent. The even-build rule requires raising the lowest set first, so I will build one house on Atlantic for $150 and then add one more house to any other yellow property.

I will build one house on Atlantic for $150, leaving $489. Two houses on every yellow property would cost $600 and leave only $39, which is too risky against a $200 railroad rent and a potential hotel. The jump from one house to two is severe enough to bankrupt player 2, so I will not overbuild.

I am now weighing the opportunity cost of building. A single house on Atlantic would leave $489, which is safer than the $189 left by a two-house build. I also noted that unmortgaging Boardwalk costs $220.

Unmortgaging Boardwalk would only double Park Place rent from $35 to $70. Player 2 is already on Boardwalk and passed the space, so no rent was collected. Building houses there would leave only $19 cash, which is too risky. I will not unmortgage Boardwalk now.

Unmortgaging the orange properties would cost $198 and yield only a small rent increase, so that path is abandoned. I am now considering trades with player 2 and player 3. I also notice that North Carolina is unowned and the green monopoly is incomplete.

I will not trade Mediterranean Avenue to player 3 because that would complete the brown monopoly and let them build a hotel immediately. Player 3 will not trade Illinois to me since it blocks player 2's red set. I am now checking whether player 2 might offer something useful.

Player 2's holdings include St Charles, Virginia, Kentucky, Indiana, Pacific, both utilities, and two jail cards. I do not need jail cards or utilities. Selling a property to player 2 would not complete any color set for me because the remaining pieces are blocked by player 3.

Player 3 will not sell Illinois or States because they block player 2 and have no cash need. Player 2 only has $312, so extracting cash from them is pointless. I am unsure whether a rejected trade proposal consumes the turn action.

Mortgaging Park Place would raise cash to $814, allowing four yellow houses to be built for $600 and leaving $214. That barely covers the $200 railroad rent. I am now checking whether multiple actions are permitted in one turn.

I confirmed that post-turn actions can be taken one at a time, but I will only perform one action now. Mortgaging Park Place would sacrifice its $35 rent and the ability to quickly complete the dark blue set, since Boardwalk must also be unmortgaged before any houses can be built there.

Player 2 has $982 in total liquidity from cash and mortgaged properties, so two houses on the yellow set would not bankrupt him. Three houses would raise rent to $800 on Atlantic and $850 on Ventnor and Marvin, which could be dangerous.

A hotel on Atlantic Avenue would bankrupt player 2, since his total liquidity is only $982. However, building hotels would cost $1950, which exceeds my available cash. I cannot afford to reach that level.

I cannot build three houses on every yellow property. That would cost $1050, but I only have $639 and can raise about $305 by mortgaging three properties. I can buy six more houses for $900 and leave $44. This gives me eight total houses on the three yellow properties.

I will build three houses on two yellow properties and two on the third, spending $900 and leaving only $44. That is too risky because player 3's hotels cost $550 to $600. I will wait for player 3 to land on light blue instead. It takes about four to five turns to reach Oriental Avenue from St James Place.

The path from St James Place to Oriental Avenue passes four railroads and two tax spaces. The B&O, Short Line, Reading RR, and Pennsylvania Ave all charge $200 or more. Player 3 will likely collect that rent before reaching light blue.

I am now considering chance cards as a risk. If I spend down to $44, the B&O railroad hit in one or two turns would bankrupt me unless I sell houses at half price. Selling houses to pay rent is painful and may be forced by the engine. The binding constraints before hotels are the $200 railroads and the $100 luxury tax.

A moderate build is safer than an all-in approach. Building one house on Atlantic Avenue for $150 leaves $489, which easily covers the $200 railroad rent and two bad rolls. The rent on Atlantic rises from $44 to $110, and the house will be waiting when player 2 lands. Player 2 is about four turns away from landing on yellow.

Player 3 is in jail with one failed doubles roll behind them. They need roughly sixteen spaces to reach yellow after release, so the houses will be relevant in about three to four opponent turns. Building now is correct timing rather than premature. The next step is determining the exact number of houses to place.

Two houses on every yellow property would raise rent to $330, $360, and $360. Player 2 has only $312 in cash, so he would need to mortgage to pay. Player 3 has $3508, so the rent is negligible against him. Building four houses costs $600 and leaves $39. That is too little to cover the $200 B&O railroad hit in nine spaces, which has roughly an 11% chance of occurring. Selling three houses at half price would raise about $450, enough to pay the $200 rent.

Building three houses would leave $189, still $11 short of the B&O railroad rent. Building two houses leaves $339 and avoids that shortfall. The expected cost of the 11% chance of hitting the B&O is roughly $25 in house sales.

I will build one house on Atlantic Avenue for $150. This leaves $489 in cash, which is safer than the $339 from two houses and still covers the upcoming B&O railroad hit. I can add more houses later if cash allows.

The available actions only list Atlantic Avenue as buildable. I will place one house on Atlantic and wait for the next turn to add more.

Expected rent from the next few spaces is only about $31, so cash will remain comfortable. The Short Line railroad hit is unlikely since it is nineteen spaces away. I should have over $400 when approaching hotels.

The cash and mortgaged properties still cover the $600 hotel cost without selling any houses. Liquidation backup is now $794, which is more than enough.

I recall a prior turn where I skipped building hotels because pure cash would fall below $600. Liquidation cover was higher then, so the current one-house build is safe.

The prior conservative cash rule was meant for a hotel reachable in one roll. Hotels are now thirty spaces away, so passing GO adds $200 before any hotel rent is collected. The liquidation cover of $794 and the cash-plus-GO total of $689 both exceed the $600 hotel cost. Building is confirmed as the correct play. I will keep my public message brief and strategic.

I am reconsidering the build. Player 2 is twenty-seven spaces away, and player 3 cannot reach yellow this turn. There is no timing advantage to building now versus next turn. I could simply end my turn and preserve the full $639 cash.

I checked whether building now versus next turn changes the outcome if I land on a rent space. The cash balance ends up identical either way, so there is no timing advantage to building immediately.

I checked whether a rent payment or a Chance card could block the house build. Paying $200 from $639 leaves $439, which is still enough to build. The only relevant Chance cards are advancing to Boardwalk, which is mortgaged and collects no rent, or sending me to jail, which would delay my turn.

I am checking the turn order to confirm whether opponents move before my next turn. Player 3 is still in jail, so their arrival on yellow is delayed. Building now versus waiting for the next turn appears nearly equivalent.

The turn order is p4, p2, p3, p4. Player 2 cannot reach Atlantic Avenue from Boardwalk even with a maximum roll of twelve. Player 3 cannot reach it from jail even after release. Neither opponent can land on the yellow properties before I build again.

Building now offers no rent capture advantage over waiting. The only downside is slightly less cash if a surprise charge hits, such as a Chance card or repairs.

I realized my own rule forbids building one house on Atlantic Avenue. It requires post-build cash to exceed $600, but $489 does not. I set that rule because light blue hotels cost $600 and I wanted to pay in cash without selling houses. I will ignore this old constraint and build anyway.

I checked whether any Chance or Community Chest cards could land me on a light blue hotel before passing GO. The nearest Community Chest is seventeen spaces away, and the nearest Chance is seven. A backward move from that Chance would only return me to New York Avenue, not to light blue.

The B&O and Short Line railroads are nine spaces away, so I may pass them without paying rent. The Reading Railroad is twenty-nine spaces away, making it unlikely to hit before the light blue properties. The probability of landing on any of these railroads while passing through is low.

Expected railroad and tax costs before the hotels total roughly $120. After passing GO, cash should reach about $569. That is borderline for a $600 hotel, but liquidation cover of $305 brings the total to $874. Even if both railroads and the luxury tax hit, leaving only $189, mortgaging the three properties still yields enough to pay the hotel. Building one house on Atlantic Avenue is confirmed as the correct play.

- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.

- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

I am ready to play Monopoly.

I have $619 and am on ILLINOIS_AVENUE after paying rent to p3. My holdings include a yellow monopoly with one house on Ventnor and Marvin Gardens, plus unmortgaged properties like Atlantic Avenue and Park Place.

p1 is bankrupt. p2 has $512 and no monopolies. p3 has $3,528 and two jail turns. He owns a light blue monopoly with hotels on Oriental, Vermont, and Connecticut.

p3 also owns four railroads and the green properties States, Illinois, and Pennsylvania Avenue. The bank has 30 houses and 9 hotels remaining. I will not build this turn because it would drop my cash below the hotel cover threshold. On my next roll from Illinois, I could land on B&O Railroad for $200.

Rolling from Illinois leads to several destinations. I own Atlantic Avenue, Ventnor Avenue, and Marvin Gardens. Water Works is owned by p2, so landing there would cost up to $120. Pacific belongs to p2 with no monopoly, meaning standard rent applies. North Carolina is unowned. The biggest threats are B&O Railroad and Short Line, both costing $200.

The $200 railroad rent is easily covered by my $619 cash. I will not hit the light blue hotels this turn because I must go around the board first. I am now weighing whether to build on Atlantic Avenue, which would cost $220 for one house.

I will build one house on Atlantic Avenue to match my other yellow properties. This costs $150 and leaves me with $469. Rent on Atlantic rises from $44 to $110.

p2 would need a 12 to land on Atlantic from Virginia. p3 is in jail with two turns already served and is now attempting a third roll.

p3 cannot reach Atlantic Avenue from jail in one roll. The distance is 16 spaces, which exceeds the maximum of 12. p2 also cannot land on Ventnor or Marvin from Virginia in a single roll. Only p2 rolling a 12 to reach Atlantic remains a realistic threat.

The expected value of building on Atlantic is negligible. The $150 cost only yields a 1/36 chance of an extra $66 in rent. I will not build this turn.

I cannot reach GO from Illinois in one roll. I would land on Short Line instead. The light blue hotels are at the start of the board, so I must go around first. If I land on Go to Jail, I will be safe from those hotels for a while.

A roll of 12 lands on Short Line for $200. From there, an 11-space roll could reach Oriental for $600. Building Atlantic would leave only $269 after that hit. I need to keep roughly $600 cash before entering the light blue danger zone.

I mapped the exact sequence from Illinois. Rolling 2 lands on B&O Railroad for $200. Rolling 3 lands on Atlantic Avenue. Rolling 4 lands on Ventnor Avenue. Rolling 5 lands on Water Works, costing only $50 because p2 owns both utilities. Rolling 6 lands on Marvin Gardens. Rolling 7 lands on Go to Jail.

Rolling 9 from Illinois lands on North Carolina, an unowned green property priced at $300. I can afford to buy it.

I will buy North Carolina. It is a trade chip that blocks p3 from completing his green monopoly and prevents p2 from acquiring Pacific cheaply.

The $600 cash rule is for paying light blue hotels without selling houses. Post-build cash would be $469, which does not clear that threshold. Mortgageable holdings total $305.

Cash plus mortgageable holdings totals $924, comfortably above the $600 hotel threshold. Building one house on Atlantic would leave $774, still above that mark. The earlier $200 rule applied to a second-house tier.

I will not build on Atlantic this turn. Post-build cash would drop to $469, below the $600 threshold. The light blue hotels are still far away from my current position on Illinois Avenue. I will wait until after p2 and p3 finish their turns and I roll again.

I will not buy North Carolina now. The action state does not include a buy option, and I can decide later if I land there.

I am reconsidering the $150 house on Atlantic. p2 is on Virginia and can only reach Atlantic with a roll of 12.

I realized I must build before p2's turn so the rent applies. If I build now and end my turn, p2 rolling a 5 from Virginia would land on New York Avenue. I own all three orange properties, but St James and Tennessee are mortgaged, so no rent is collected there.

Standard Monopoly rules confirm that a color group cannot collect doubled rent while any property in it is mortgaged. Because St James and Tennessee are mortgaged, New York Avenue would only pay base rent. I also cannot build houses on the orange set until all three properties are unmortgaged.

Unmortgaging both orange properties would cost $198. That money is better spent on the yellow houses already in place. p2 can land on New York Avenue for only $16 base rent, so unmortgaging is not worthwhile.

Atlantic's one-house rent is $110, a $66 increase over the base $44. Yellow is a frequent landing spot for players coming out of jail. The liquidity constraint remains the main issue. p3's hotels are the primary threat. I am weighing whether to build high enough on yellow to bankrupt p2 or survive p3's hotels.

p3 can reach Atlantic Avenue from jail in two rolls. After leaving jail on spaces 12 through 22, a roll of 5 or 4 lands them on Atlantic. This makes the one-house rent jump to $110 worthwhile.

The turn sequence confirms p3 cannot reach yellow on the same turn they leave jail. After my next roll from Illinois, I will have another post-turn decision before p3 can land on yellow.

I will not build on Atlantic now. The missed rent from p2 is too small to justify the $150 liquidity risk.

I am now considering a trade with p2 or p3. I own both dark blue properties, but Boardwalk is mortgaged and cannot be developed until unmortgaged. Unmortgaging it would cost $220, leaving me with $399.

Unmortgaging Boardwalk would leave only $399, which is too little to build evenly on dark blue. Unmortgaging the orange properties would leave $421 after paying $198, but that money is better spent on yellow houses to protect against hotel hits.

I will not trade Mediterranean Avenue to p3, since that would let them complete the brown monopoly and hotel it. p2 has two jail cards, but p3 is about to leave jail anyway, so those cards are not a useful trade chip.

Jail cards are less useful now that p3 is leaving jail. Staying in jail late game could avoid hotel hits, but p2 will not trade cheaply for them. I cannot offer p2 a monopoly since I lack the missing pieces. p3 might want Mediterranean Avenue to complete the brown set, though I would need to give up both dark blue properties to let them finish the dark blue set.

p3 cannot complete the orange set, so they would not trade for it. A brown hotel at $250 is less threatening than light blue hotels at $550–600, but giving p3 another hotel strip is too risky. I would lose Mediterranean Avenue as a mortgage buffer and property. p3 has no incentive to trade away their assets. I am now exploring whether a trade with p2 could hurt p3.

I will end my turn. Buying Pacific would not block p3 from completing green, since North Carolina is unowned and the rent is too low to justify spending cash.

prompt_messages.content:
You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

message.reasoning:
I am ready to play Monopoly as grok-4.

I have $591 and am on Pennsylvania Avenue after paying $28 rent. I own all three orange properties but two are mortgaged, so I cannot build houses there yet. I also own Ventnor Avenue with one house and Atlantic Avenue with none.

Marvin Gardens has one house, so I can only build on Atlantic to even the yellow set. I also own Park Place unmortgaged and Boardwalk mortgaged. Player 1 is bankrupt. Player 2 has $512 and no monopolies.

Player 3 has $3,506 and owns all four railroads. They have hotels on the light blue set and own states and illinois to block player 2's monopolies. The bank has thirty houses and nine hotels. I am deciding what action to take next.

I will not unmortgage the orange properties or Boardwalk because that would break my hotel cover buffer. I am checking whether I can build on Atlantic Avenue while still keeping at least $600 in cash after construction, since light-blue hotels cost $550 to $600.

Player 3 is on the Pennsylvania Railroad. The turn order skips the bankrupt player, so I will end my turn and let player 2 play next.

I am calculating my next roll. A twelve would land me on Oriental Avenue with its hotel, costing $550. I can afford it and would still have $41 left.

I cannot build on Atlantic Avenue. Doing so would leave me with only $441, which falls short of the $600 hotel cover buffer. I will skip building and end my turn.

I could sell both yellow houses for $150, raising my cash to about $741. Player 3 is the dominant threat with light-blue hotels and all four railroads, so I am considering a trade proposal.

Player 2's assets are incomplete monopolies on the red and green sets. I am weighing whether to trade my orange properties to player 2, but that would create a second builder who could also hit me. Player 3's light-blue hotels pay $550 on Oriental and $600 each on Vermont and Connecticut.

Player 3's next roll from the Pennsylvania Railroad would hit my yellow properties on an 11 or 12. Expected rent is only about $4.8, rising to roughly $6.1 if I build on Atlantic Avenue.

Player 2 is on Free Parking. He can land on my yellow properties on a roll of six, seven, or nine. Expected rent from him is roughly $39.

Building one house on Atlantic Avenue would only raise expected rent by about twelve dollars, so it is not worth the one-hundred-fifty-dollar cost. To reach two houses on every yellow property would require six hundred dollars total. Player three will likely bankrupt me unless I can build a serious threat.

Even three houses on every yellow property would cost $1,050. I cannot afford that without mortgaging everything and still falling short. Selling existing buildings would not raise enough cash to rebuild elsewhere.

I cannot build a threatening monopoly with my current cash. I will either trade to complete a cheaper high-rent set or wait for player 3 to hit another property and bleed.

Player 3 might want Mediterranean Avenue to complete the brown set. A brown hotel would pay only about $250, which is less threatening than their existing light-blue hotels. Selling it could raise enough cash to build three houses on every yellow property.

A brown hotel would pay only about $250 on Mediterranean and $450 on Baltic, so player 3 might not pay a large premium for it. Still, player 3 has excess cash and could buy it to deny me a trade chip or complete the set. Selling Mediterranean for roughly four hundred to eight hundred dollars would raise my cash to about one thousand two hundred ninety-one dollars.

Even with roughly $1,291, three houses on every yellow property would leave only about $241. Player 3’s light-blue hotels pay $550 to $600, so a single hit nearly wipes me. I cannot survive many of those hits before my yellow set pays off. The trade is too risky.

Mortgaging more would leave me with only about two hundred ninety-six dollars after a single hotel hit, so I cannot survive two. Player two is also fragile and will land on railroads often. The only viable path to victory is a trade that gives me both a completed high-rent monopoly and enough cash to stay safe.

Three houses on every orange property would pay about five hundred to six hundred dollars each. That is comparable to player three's light-blue hotels, and the set is landed on frequently after jail. Player two could use it as a strong threat against player three.

I am now considering trading with player three instead. Player two already owns Pacific Avenue and North Carolina, so he could complete the green set with Pennsylvania Avenue. Player three might also trade Illinois or States to help player two build a pink monopoly.

Baltic Avenue would give me a brown monopoly, but hotels there pay only about two hundred fifty and four hundred fifty dollars. Building both sets would cost five hundred dollars, leaving me with ninety-one dollars after the purchase. That is too little cash to threaten player three, so this trade is unappealing.

Player three wants Mediterranean Avenue to complete the brown set, not to sell it. I cannot trade my yellow monopoly for cash or other useful pieces, since Illinois and States do not help me and a railroad would not win the game. Player two has no dark blue properties, so he would not want Boardwalk or Park Place. I will keep my yellow set intact.

I cannot build on dark blue while Boardwalk is mortgaged. The only safe play is to end my turn and preserve the $591 cash buffer.

A trade proposal is the only remaining path to victory. Three houses on every yellow property would charge $800 to $900 per hit, which exceeds player three's light-blue hotels at $550 to $600. Player three lands on orange and light blue more often than on yellow because jail exits frequently land there. This makes a yellow monopoly a stronger long-term threat than player three's current holdings.

A new trade proposal is forming: offer Mediterranean Avenue to player three for roughly eight hundred dollars, then use that cash to build three houses on every yellow property. This would create a strong threat against player three while player two could be convinced to damage player three.

Player three is unlikely to pay eight hundred dollars for Mediterranean Avenue. That money would fund my yellow houses, which are more dangerous than brown hotels. They might offer two hundred to three hundred dollars instead, which still falls short of the one thousand fifty dollars needed for three houses on every yellow property. Even four hundred dollars would leave me with only nine hundred ninety-one dollars, barely enough to reach two houses.

Two houses on every yellow property would pay only three hundred thirty to three hundred ninety dollars per hit. That is too weak to threaten player three's light-blue hotels, and it leaves me exposed.

I will not trade away a monopoly to player two for cash or jail cards. Utilities are not worth giving up a critical piece for.

I am now re-reading the win condition.

Player two has no monopoly and only earns low utility rent. He will bleed to player three's railroads and light-blue hotels. I have slightly more cash and mortgage liquidity, so I might outlast him. Then it is me against player three, who will win unless I develop.

I must develop either yellow or orange to survive the endgame. The next roll carries a moderate expected loss of about one hundred dollars. I can afford the worst single hit, but building would leave me unable to pay an Oriental hotel and would force me to mortgage. Mortgaging during rent payment might be automatic.

Proposing a trade is not mutually exclusive with ending the turn later. I am now weighing whether player two would accept cash and jail cards in exchange for orange properties, which would arm him as a threat against player three.

That leaves him with only about one hundred fourteen dollars, which is too little cash to threaten player three immediately. A trade that arms player two would not help me survive the endgame, so this path is unappealing.

Arming player two would create a dangerous two-player threat against me. I am now checking whether any trade could let another player complete a set, but splitting dark blue or trading Illinois would not help.

I will not trade away any color set to player three, since that would arm them with a monster monopoly. Player two could also use orange or yellow to threaten me, so those pieces must stay too.

Selling dark blue to player two for cash and jail cards would give me about one thousand thirteen dollars. That is enough to build three houses on every yellow property, but it would leave me with no cash buffer afterward.

- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.

- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

prompt_messages.content:
You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.

- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.

- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

message.reasoning:
I need to make a Monopoly decision.

I have $901 and a yellow monopoly with one house on Ventnor and Marvin. I can build on Atlantic. Opponent p1 is bankrupt.

p2 has $512 and owns Pacific Avenue plus utilities. p3 has $3096 with hotels on the light blue set and all four railroads.

I own the full orange set with two mortgaged. I cannot build houses until both are unmortgaged.

Unmortgaging both orange properties costs $198. Unmortgaging Boardwalk costs $220. I have enough cash to cover either. I am calculating rent and house costs for the yellow set.

I calculated the exact rent for each yellow property with one house on Ventnor and Marvin. I also noted p3's light blue hotels pay $550 to $600. Next I will roll from GO, passing Mediterranean, Baltic, and Income Tax.

I mapped the full 12-space roll from GO. The worst hits are Reading Railroad, Oriental, Vermont, and Connecticut hotels. I can afford the Connecticut hotel with $301 left over. The probability of landing on an opponent's hotel is roughly 14%.

I calculated the expected rent from rolling from GO. The average cost is about $260, including tax and railroad. Building a house on Atlantic Avenue costs $150. After that I would have $751 left. That still clears the $600 Connecticut hotel. I will build the house.

I checked standard Monopoly rules. The monopoly double-rent bonus applies only when no buildings are on any property of the group. Since Ventnor and Marvin already have houses, Atlantic would collect base rent rather than doubled rent.

Atlantic rent rises from $26 to $130 with one house. I am checking which opponent can land there before my next turn.

Neither opponent can land on Atlantic before my next turn. p2 is on Pacific and would need to pass GO, which is 35 spaces away. p3 is on North Carolina and cannot reach the yellow set in one roll. Building a house now would not generate rent before the hotel risk.

Building now versus after the roll yields the same cash outcome if I survive the hotel. The house would sit idle until after my roll anyway, since neither opponent can land on Atlantic before then.

I am now weighing whether to unmortgage the orange set instead. That would cost $198 and leave me with $703, but I still cannot build houses until both properties are unmortgaged.

Unmortgaging the orange set costs $498 and leaves only $403, which is too low to survive the upcoming hotel. Unmortgaging Boardwalk leaves $681, but the mortgaged Boardwalk still collects no rent, so that path offers little benefit. Building the house on Atlantic remains the best play.

Only one house can be built on Atlantic Avenue. I am now considering a trade with p3 to acquire Mediterranean Avenue and complete the brown set.

I rejected trading Mediterranean Avenue to p3 because that would give them hotels on Baltic and Mediterranean, adding more kill shots. p2 wants States, Illinois, and North Carolina to complete his pink, red, and green sets. I do not own those missing pieces. I am now considering offering my orange monopoly to p2.

I see three paths to victory. Build the yellow set high enough to hurt p3 when they land. Unmortgage Boardwalk and build dark blue houses, though that is expensive. Or ally with p2 to attack p3 together.

p3 now owns two green properties. If they acquire Pacific Avenue from p2, they will have a green monopoly and can hotel it to end the game. I should try to get Pacific from p2 before p3 does. I could offer p2 a property in exchange for Pacific. Pacific blocks p3's green set. I need to find something p2 wants.

I am calculating the rent from an orange house on New York Avenue. That would yield $160. I am also checking p3's position on North Carolina.

I cannot land on orange this roll because the maximum move is twelve spaces. I will not face orange rent until my next turn. I am now weighing the risk of giving p2 the orange monopoly. That would let them extract money from p3, but they could also hit me with orange rent and light blue hotels.

I am now calculating the exact cost of giving p2 the orange set. Unmortgaging New York and St. James would cost $198, then one house on each property would add another $300, leaving only about $14 in cash. That is too little to build immediately.

Instead, I will keep the orange set for myself and unmortgage it later when the danger passes.

For Pacific Avenue, I am preparing a bid that includes cash plus another property. p2 cannot complete the green set on his own, so he may be willing to sell. I need to outbid p3 before they acquire it.

Pacific Avenue is a pure blocker with no rent. It is worth the cash only to stop p3 from completing a green monopoly and hoteling it for $1,400 to $1,500. I will offer p2 cash for Pacific.

A cash-only offer for Pacific Avenue is hopeless. p3 has $3,096 and can outbid me easily. I need to offer p2 a property he actually wants, such as my orange monopoly or States and Illinois, so he will not sell Pacific to p3.

I decided against trading the orange monopoly to p2. That set is my own path to victory, not just survival. I will keep it and continue building on yellow.

I will build the house on Atlantic Avenue first. I can afford it now that my cash clears the $600 reserve. I will reassess after this turn.

I confirmed that selling houses on Ventnor and Marvin would recover $75 each, giving me enough liquidity to survive a hotel hit. I will keep my public message brief and strategic. I am now drafting the exact build_plan JSON for the house on Atlantic Avenue.

I will keep the private thought brief and strategic. After building the house on Atlantic Avenue, I will have $751 in cash. That covers the $600 hotel reserve, so I will not unmortgage anything yet. I also rejected trading Mediterranean Avenue to p3 or the orange set to p2. The next tier of yellow houses would cost $450, which I may not afford if I survive with only $151 left.

A bad roll would leave me with only $301 to $351. That is too little to build a house and still survive the next hotel. A roll of 2 would land me on Community Chest, leaving the hotels still ahead. I must build now while I have enough cash.

I am now calculating the exact landing spots for each possible roll. A roll of 6 would land me on the hotel and clear the danger for this lap. A roll of 7 would leave the hotels partially ahead, while a roll of 10 or higher would place them behind me. I also realized that each turn is a single landing, so I only pay rent for where I actually land.

I realized the hotel danger is actually my next turn, not this one. I have already resolved my movement and am now in the post-turn phase, so I will roll from GO on my upcoming turn.

reasoning_details.summary:
I need to make a Monopoly decision.

I have $901 and a yellow monopoly with one house on Ventnor and Marvin. I can build on Atlantic. Opponent p1 is bankrupt.

p2 has $512 and owns Pacific Avenue plus utilities. p3 has $3096 with hotels on the light blue set and all four railroads.

I own the full orange set with two mortgaged. I cannot build houses until both are unmortgaged.

Unmortgaging both orange properties costs $198. Unmortgaging Boardwalk costs $220. I have enough cash to cover either. I am calculating rent and house costs for the yellow set.

I calculated the exact rent for each yellow property with one house on Ventnor and Marvin. I also noted p3's light blue hotels pay $550 to $600. Next I will roll from GO, passing Mediterranean, Baltic, and Income Tax.

I mapped the full 12-space roll from GO. The worst hits are Reading Railroad, Oriental, Vermont, and Connecticut hotels. I can afford the Connecticut hotel with $301 left over. The probability of landing on an opponent's hotel is roughly 14%.

I calculated the expected rent from rolling from GO. The average cost is about $260, including tax and railroad. Building a house on Atlantic Avenue costs $150. After that I would have $751 left. That still clears the $600 Connecticut hotel. I will build the house.

I checked standard Monopoly rules. The monopoly double-rent bonus applies only when no buildings are on any property of the group. Since Ventnor and Marvin already have houses, Atlantic would collect base rent rather than doubled rent.

Atlantic rent rises from $26 to $130 with one house. I am checking which opponent can land there before my next turn.

Neither opponent can land on Atlantic before my next turn. p2 is on Pacific and would need to pass GO, which is 35 spaces away. p3 is on North Carolina and cannot reach the yellow set in one roll. Building a house now would not generate rent before the hotel risk.

Building now versus after the roll yields the same cash outcome if I survive the hotel. The house would sit idle until after my roll anyway, since neither opponent can land on Atlantic before then.

I am now weighing whether to unmortgage the orange set instead. That would cost $198 and leave me with $703, but I still cannot build houses until both properties are unmortgaged.

Unmortgaging the orange set costs $498 and leaves only $403, which is too low to survive the upcoming hotel. Unmortgaging Boardwalk leaves $681, but the mortgaged Boardwalk still collects no rent, so that path offers little benefit. Building the house on Atlantic remains the best play.

Only one house can be built on Atlantic Avenue. I am now considering a trade with p3 to acquire Mediterranean Avenue and complete the brown set.

I rejected trading Mediterranean Avenue to p3 because that would give them hotels on Baltic and Mediterranean, adding more kill shots. p2 wants States, Illinois, and North Carolina to complete his pink, red, and green sets. I do not own those missing pieces. I am now considering offering my orange monopoly to p2.

I see three paths to victory. Build the yellow set high enough to hurt p3 when they land. Unmortgage Boardwalk and build dark blue houses, though that is expensive. Or ally with p2 to attack p3 together.

p3 now owns two green properties. If they acquire Pacific Avenue from p2, they will have a green monopoly and can hotel it to end the game. I should try to get Pacific from p2 before p3 does. I could offer p2 a property in exchange for Pacific. Pacific blocks p3's green set. I need to find something p2 wants.

I am calculating the rent from an orange house on New York Avenue. That would yield $160. I am also checking p3's position on North Carolina.

I cannot land on orange this roll because the maximum move is twelve spaces. I will not face orange rent until my next turn. I am now weighing the risk of giving p2 the orange monopoly. That would let them extract money from p3, but they could also hit me with orange rent and light blue hotels.

I am now calculating the exact cost of giving p2 the orange set. Unmortgaging New York and St. James would cost $198, then one house on each property would add another $300, leaving only about $14 in cash. That is too little to build immediately.

Instead, I will keep the orange set for myself and unmortgage it later when the danger passes.

For Pacific Avenue, I am preparing a bid that includes cash plus another property. p2 cannot complete the green set on his own, so he may be willing to sell. I need to outbid p3 before they acquire it.

Pacific Avenue is a pure blocker with no rent. It is worth the cash only to stop p3 from completing a green monopoly and hoteling it for $1,400 to $1,500. I will offer p2 cash for Pacific.

A cash-only offer for Pacific Avenue is hopeless. p3 has $3,096 and can outbid me easily. I need to offer p2 a property he actually wants, such as my orange monopoly or States and Illinois, so he will not sell Pacific to p3.

I decided against trading the orange monopoly to p2. That set is my own path to victory, not just survival. I will keep it and continue building on yellow.

I will build the house on Atlantic Avenue first. I can afford it now that my cash clears the $600 reserve. I will reassess after this turn.

I confirmed that selling houses on Ventnor and Marvin would recover $75 each, giving me enough liquidity to survive a hotel hit. I will keep my public message brief and strategic. I am now drafting the exact build_plan JSON for the house on Atlantic Avenue.

I will keep the private thought brief and strategic. After building the house on Atlantic Avenue, I will have $751 in cash. That covers the $600 hotel reserve, so I will not unmortgage anything yet. I also rejected trading Mediterranean Avenue to p3 or the orange set to p2. The next tier of yellow houses would cost $450, which I may not afford if I survive with only $151 left.

A bad roll would leave me with only $301 to $351. That is too little to build a house and still survive the next hotel. A roll of 2 would land me on Community Chest, leaving the hotels still ahead. I must build now while I have enough cash.

I am now calculating the exact landing spots for each possible roll. A roll of 6 would land me on the hotel and clear the danger for this lap. A roll of 7 would leave the hotels partially ahead, while a roll of 10 or higher would place them behind me. I also realized that each turn is a single landing, so I only pay rent for where I actually land.

I realized the hotel danger is actually my next turn, not this one. I have already resolved my movement and am now in the post-turn phase, so I will roll from GO on my upcoming turn.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.

- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

prompt_messages.content:
You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

prompt_messages.content:
You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

prompt_messages.content:
You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.
